canonical_statement: The study evaluated seven widely accessible LLM configurations on real-world Thai-language drug information questions, focusing on concordance with pharmacist responses, Thai-language clarity, relevance, context awareness, and citation credibility.
Investigators included 102 eligible drug information questions retrieved from 2024-2025 records of a university-hospital drug information center in Thailand.

population.label: 102 eligible historical Thai-language drug information questions from a university hospital drug information center; seven LLM responses per question

canonical_statement: Eligible records addressed dosage, administration, special populations, stability or compatibility, drug interactions, adverse effects, vaccines, or therapeutic use.

population.label: Historical DIC records

canonical_statement: Records were excluded for product availability, cost, drug identification, or when required patient information was insufficient.

population.label: Historical DIC records

canonical_statement: All eligible questions and corresponding pharmacist responses were originally documented in Thai, and LLM responses were generated and evaluated in Thai.

The evaluation instrument defined five domains: concordance, clarity, relevance, context awareness, and citation credibility; pharmacist-provided responses were the reference standard only for concordance.
Concordance, relevance, context awareness, and citation credibility were scored as binary outcomes, while clarity used a 5-point Likert scale.

Three experts representing clinical pharmacy, evidence-based practice, and health-related research assessed content validity using the index of item-objective congruence before the rubric was finalized.
The study evaluated seven LLM configurations: ChatGPT-5.2 Instant, ChatGPT-5.2 Thinking, Gemini 3 Fast, Gemini 3 Thinking, Perplexity Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Copilot Think Deeper.
Each question was placed into a standardized drug-information prompt that asked the model to consider Thai medication use and treatment guidance and to provide references with accessible links.

Investigators opened a new chat session for each inquiry, generated all responses in November 2025, preserved the original question wording except for minor formatting, and did not add clinical context.
The pilot reliability phase used 10 questions submitted to all seven LLMs, producing 70 responses that three assessors rated independently for 210 rating instances.

population.label: 70 LLM responses generated from 10 pilot questions and rated independently by three assessors

canonical_statement: After the pilot reliability assessment, investigators split the 102 main questions into three subsets and assigned each subset to one assessor, so each main-study response received one assessor rating.

population.label: 714 LLM responses generated from 102 eligible Thai-language drug information questions

canonical_statement: Investigators treated binary-domain fulfillment of at least 0.80 as acceptable, compared seven models with Cochran Q tests, used McNemar tests with Holm adjustment after significant omnibus tests, and expressed mean clarity scores as a percentage of the 5-point maximum.
Free-text assessor comments were reviewed to classify citation problems as hallucinated or irrelevant sources, inaccessible links, non-academic sources, or non-specific citations.
Pilot inter-rater agreement for concordance was 0.84, interpreted by the study as almost perfect agreement.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that LLMs may help with preliminary drug-information retrieval and response drafting, but pharmacist review remains necessary for clinical accuracy, interpretation, and source verification.
The authors stated that better citation transparency and source attribution are needed before broader clinical integration.
The single-center tertiary-hospital DIC setting may limit generalizability to other health-care settings.
The number and scope of evaluated questions may not represent the full diversity of clinical drug-information queries.
Performance depends on the evaluated model versions and may change with model updates.
A single standardized prompt was used, so results may not represent other real-world prompting strategies or optimized prompting.
Binary scoring for four domains may not capture partial correctness or other nuances of response quality.
Although pilot agreement was high, each response in the main analysis was evaluated by one assessor, so residual rater variability cannot be excluded.
The study did not systematically classify which source types pharmacists used in the original DIC responses, limiting analysis by evidence requirement.
The evaluation excluded specialized medical LLMs, proprietary clinical AI, and institution-specific retrieval-augmented systems.

Ashley M. Hopkins reported investigator-initiated research funding outside this study from Boehringer Ingelheim and speaker fees from AstraZeneca; the other authors declared no conflicts of interest.
The authors stated that study data are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
The authors reported using ChatGPT-5.2 for language editing and grammar only, with no AI tools used for data analysis or interpretation.
Supporting Table S1 provides the complete scoring rubric, and Supporting Table S2 lists all 102 drug-information questions used in the main evaluation.
